abstract: Bick, Blandin, Deming and Schumacher build the first nationally representative, task-level measures of generative AI adoption, using four quarterly waves of the Real-Time Population Survey (August 2025 to May 2026, nearly 14,000 workers). Each worker reports their detailed occupation, which of their occupation's ten most important O*NET detailed work activities they perform, and which of those genAI helps with. The resulting occupation- and task-level adoption indexes show adoption that is widespread but shallow: four in five occupations have adoption above 20%, but only one in six exceed 70%, and no task exceeds 70%. Standard AI exposure scores explain between 5% and 53% of adoption variation across occupations and 7% to 44% across tasks, with clerical and administrative work adopting far less than predicted and high-autonomy work more. Task measures built from Anthropic, OpenAI and Microsoft chat logs disagree with the survey and with each other, which the authors attribute to classifiers that cannot see the user's occupation and so over-assign generic activity tasks.
keyFindings: Exposure scores predict between 5% and 53% of adoption variation across occupations and 7% to 44% across tasks
Widespread: at least 20% of workers use AI in more than 80% of occupations and on more than 40% of job tasks
Shallow: at least half of workers use AI in only 40% of occupations and for less than 3% of job tasks; 16% of occupations and no task exceed 70% adoption
Highest-adoption occupations: computer and information research scientists (87.3%), information security analysts (85.4%), network and computer systems administrators (82.4%)
Lowest-adoption occupations: animal caretakers (5.3%), receptionists and information clerks (7.6%), licensed practical and vocational nurses (10.4%)

Medical secretaries and administrative assistants use AI at 16.8% against a predicted 61%; computer repairers (75.7%), special education teachers (70.9%) and laundry workers (49.0%) adopt at roughly double their predicted rate

Chat-log task measures (Anthropic, OpenAI, Microsoft) correlate below 0.4 pairwise; more than 15% of OpenAI chats are classed as 'Edit written materials or documents' though only 2.4% of workers are in occupations with that task
Workers with six or more months of genAI experience use it for more tasks, consistent with a learning mechanism that predicts adoption will deepen over time
methodology: Real-Time Population Survey, an online CPS-mirroring survey of US adults 18-64 fielded by Qualtrics and weighted to be nationally representative. In the 08/25, 11/25, 02/26 and 05/26 waves, respondents' free-text job titles are coded to 2018 SOC occupations; respondents are shown their occupation's ten most important O*NET detailed work activities, report which they perform, and report which genAI regularly helps with. Occupation adoption = share of workers in the occupation using genAI for work; task adoption = share of workers performing the task who use genAI for it. Indexes are compared with Eloundou et al., Felten et al., Webb and Brynjolfsson et al. exposure scores and with chat-log task shares from Handa et al. (Anthropic), Chatterji et al. (OpenAI) and Tomlinson et al. (Microsoft). Indexes are downloadable at sites.google.com/view/covid-rps/data and will be updated with future waves.
qualifiers: Tier 1 - Federal Reserve working paper (St. Louis Fed WP 2026-017; also NBER w35677), not yet peer-reviewed. Adoption is self-reported and pooled over four waves, so the indexes describe August 2025-May 2026 rather than the current wave. Only an occupation's ten most important O*NET tasks are shown, which the authors validate against economy-wide task shares but which omits less central tasks. The indexes measure whether AI is used for a task, not how much of the task it performs, so they are not a measure of automation or displacement. Occupation cells with few respondents are noisy; the paper requires at least 10 observations per title.
